analysis.one_liner: Requires warehouses to disclose worker quotas, guarantee paid breaks, and limit surveillance-driven discipline.
analysis.headline: The warehouse quota and safety bill was referred to the Senate labor committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required warehouse companies to tell workers, in writing, exactly what production quotas they face and what surveillance technology is used to track them. It would ban quotas that cut into legally required breaks or bathroom time, mandate a paid 15-minute rest break every four hours, require written notice before firing a quota-covered worker, let workers see and dispute their own speed-tracking data, and bar companies from forcing quota disputes into private arbitration. It would also direct OSHA to write ergonomic-injury and medical-referral standards for warehouses and give the Labor Department money to inspect facilities with high injury rates. It never got past the referral stage.
analysis.who_benefits: Warehouse and fulfillment-center workers subject to production quotas, who would gain written disclosure of their quotas, paid breaks, the right to see and dispute their speed data, protection from retaliation, and access to ergonomic and medical-referral protections. Unions and worker advocacy groups would gain a formal role in enforcement and inspections.

how_it_helps.text: Covered employers would have to give each worker a written description of every quota, including the disciplinary consequences of missing it, how targets are calculated, and what surveillance technology is used to collect work-speed data [S2].

Employers could not impose quotas that prevent legally required meal or rest breaks, use of bathroom facilities with travel time, or reasonable accommodations, and could not discipline workers for failing quotas that were never disclosed [S2].
Workers would receive one paid 15-minute rest break for every four hours of work, with notice and signage in the worker's primary language [S2].
Before firing any quota-covered worker, employers would have to give written notice, and firings tied to work-speed data would require providing that data in human-readable form [S2].

Workers could review their work-speed data, annotate breaks and injuries, request corrections, and get their data and similarly situated coworkers' aggregated data at no cost within seven business days [S2].

Quota-related claims could not be forced into predispute arbitration or subject to class-action waivers, and an employee suing on behalf of similarly situated workers would be treated as meeting the usual class prerequisites [S2].

The Labor Department would be required to open an on-site investigation of any warehouse employer with 40,000+ annual work hours and an injury rate at least 1.5 times the warehousing industry average, or after repeated credible complaints [S2].
OSHA would be directed to issue standards on ergonomic hazards causing musculoskeletal disorders and on prompt medical referral after warehouse injuries [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large warehousing, e-commerce fulfillment, wholesale distribution, and parcel companies, plus the staffing agencies that supply them. They would bear disclosure, recordkeeping, and paid-break costs, new civil penalties of up to roughly $77,000 per violation (and more for willful or repeat violations), OSHA compliance costs for ergonomics and onsite medical consultation, and restrictions on how they use productivity surveillance.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large warehousing and e-commerce fulfillment companies

drawbacks.text: Paid-break mandates, recordkeeping, and compliance with new OSHA ergonomics standards would raise operating costs for logistics companies, some of which could be passed to consumers through higher prices [S2].

The bill prohibits evaluating output over any period shorter than a day and penalizes discipline based on rankings against other workers or the worker's own past performance, which goes beyond preventing abusive quotas and would constrain ordinary performance-management tools many employers consider legitimate [S2].

Data-minimization rules would limit how employers use tracking information even for purposes unrelated to punishing workers, and the definition of covered employers sweeps in contractors, staffing agencies, and courier services, broadening compliance burdens across the supply chain [S2].

The bill contains no offsetting deregulation or cost relief, and its authorization of appropriations for fiscal years 2025 through 2035 is unlimited ('such sums as may be necessary'), which opponents would flag as an open-ended federal expense [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is an unusually detailed pro-worker proposal aimed at a specific, well-documented problem: algorithmic production quotas and injury rates in warehouse work. The protections it offers — disclosed quotas, paid breaks, access to one's own tracking data, an end to forced arbitration for quota claims — respond directly to how these jobs are managed. The strongest honest objections are cost and overreach: the compliance and penalty regime would be expensive for logistics firms, and the ban on sub-daily output measurement and ranking-based discipline constrains legitimate performance management, not just abuse. On balance the design is targeted rather than sloppy, but its breadth across contractors and couriers means the cost side is real.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced S. 4260 on May 2, 2024, joined by original cosponsors Casey, Smith, and Brown [S1][S2].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction [S4].
Ten senators cosponsored the bill; all were Democrats or Independents, with no Republican support listed [S3].
No further action was recorded after the referral — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote appears in the action history through the end of the Congress [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large warehouse, e-commerce, and parcel companies are better off: they continue to operate under no federal quota-disclosure, paid-break, or surveillance limits, and no OSHA ergonomics mandate was set in motion. Workers who would have gained these protections got nothing.

industries.industry: Warehousing and e-commerce fulfillment (incl. parcel and courier services)
industries.note: The bill imposes quota disclosure, paid breaks, data-access rights, arbitration bans, and civil penalties of up to $76,987 per violation ($769,870 for willful or repeat violations) on covered facilities, and directs OSHA to write ergonomics standards. Its profit model of maximizing task throughput at low cost would be constrained in ways that directly protect the workers it manages.
Staffing agencies and employee-leasing entities are expressly included as covered employers, so agency-supplied warehouse workers get the same protections and the firms bear the compliance costs.

The bill requires disclosure of surveillance technology, limits data collection to what is strictly necessary for quota monitoring, and gives workers access to and correction of their speed data — shrinking both the market and the levers these systems give employers.

industries.industry: Labor unions and worker advocacy organizations
industries.note: The bill gives them standing to file and represent quota complaints, accompany federal inspectors anonymously requested by workers, and serve on the advisory board and enforcement task force.
